title: Levity
full_review:
Upon his release, a remorseful convicted murderer seeks out the sister of the young man he impulsively killed 23 years earlier in the sorrowful drama "Levity" (Sony Classics).

Freed under protest, Manual Jordan (Billy Bob Thornton) feels his crime was so terrible he is irredeemable. He doesn't believe in God or his mercy but accepts an offer of room and board from self-styled preacher Miles (Morgan Freeman). The laconic preacher runs a hardscrabble youth center with a soup kitchen and offers free evening parking to the adjacent dance club patrons if they listen to 15 minutes of his sermons. He also encourages listless Manual to get on with his post-prison life and help those around him.

Manual approaches his victim's sister, Adele (Holly Hunter), who doesn't recognize the dour-looking man with long, straggly gray hair, and gradually a tentative friendship begins. But, unable to reveal his true identity, he is stymied in getting the forgiveness he barely recognizes that he seeks from her. She's worried about her teen son Abner (Geoffrey Wigdor), who's involved with a violent gang and Manual seems to be the only one she can talk to.

More than once, young dance club patron Sofia (Kirsten Dunst) passes out after substance abuse and Manual hauls her out of the club to get her home, making no bones about how she is foolishly wasting her life with self-destructive behaviors. Nonetheless, she likes this glowering man whom no one can make smile lest exhibit any sense of humor.

Increasingly, Miles puts Manual in charge of operations during his mysterious absences, and the hesitant ex-con is forced to open up to a gang of aggressive kids he fears will likely end up in jail.

The movie's drama spikes when Abner is shot, survives, but is dead set on revenge-killing his shooter -- and Adele pleads with Manual to prevent it.

As written and directed by Ed Solomon, it's a far cry from his previous comedic writing credits, "Men in Black" and "Bill & Ted's Adventure" screenplays. Making his directorial debut, he focuses on accountability and the possibility of redemption, but without the slightest hint of, well, levity.

Thornton gives a measured, understated performance as a miserable man, haunted by what he did, who has visions of the handsome youth he shot in the head during a convenience-store robbery. While his is a good character study, the same cannot be said for the underwritten characters who surround him.

We have few clues why neither Adele or Sofia have any friends whatever, why Adele never made anything of herself or why Sofia is so disaffected. Miles' character is more satisfying as the mystery of his past is explained -- unlike the movie's end which gives little certainty about the fate of Manual, Miles, Adele and Sofia. In their own ways, each has been seeking redemption and forced to reconsider their lives, with the implication they will choose more positive directions.

After the drama's intentionally slow pace and gloomy tone, such a guardedly hopeful finish seems like a reward to the audience.

Although only Miles believes in God, the others' skepticism is belied by how they have reflected on their actions in relation to the possibility of God and an afterlife. And so one can read a spiritual dimension into this meditative film despite its apparently secular characters. Indeed, its redemptive theme is overemphasized as Manual not once but twice recites the five ingredients necessary for redemption, before concluding he does not qualify. Yet Manual becomes so righteous he is willing to sacrifice his own life to save another's and prevent Abner from following the murderous path he has taken.

Shot in Montreal, the drama looks as gray as its characters' outlooks. It is rare that a film addresses the aftermath of violence and its lifelong effects as this one does without any sugar-coating. However, its grim presentation and not-truly-fleshed-out characters will try viewer patience, and those looking for its spiritual side may be put off by the preponderance of four-letter words.

Due to recurring rough language, minimal profanity, an implied sexual encounter and some crass expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
